# The kernel card

The whole grammar, on one page. The table below is extracted from [The
kernel](grammar.qmd#the-kernel) each time the book builds. It cannot disagree
with the chapter it comes from. Functions that act on a plot instead of joining
a sentence are in [Functions around the grammar](utilities.qmd).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
# The kernel is a table, not a monospace listing, so the rows are emitted as
# markdown rather than wrapped in a code fence. Wrapping a table in ``` would
# print its pipes and asterisks at the reader.
g <- readLines("grammar.qmd")
start <- grep("^## The kernel", g)[1]
rest  <- g[start:length(g)]
end   <- which(!grepl("^\\|", rest) & nzchar(trimws(rest)) & seq_along(rest) > 2)[1]
cat(rest[seq_len(end)][grepl("^\\|", rest[seq_len(end)])], sep = "\n")
```

**The minimum sentence** is a source, a mark, and the position channels that
mark needs:

```
data(table) + mark + x(column) + y(column)
```

**The order of `+`** is mostly free: every sentence in this book reads left to
right as *data, mark, positions, refinements*. Inside one layer the mark and its
channels may be written in any order. `data()` comes first, and `style()` comes
after the mark it styles. What the order does change is scope and layering. A
channel written before any mark applies to every layer that can accept it. A
channel written after a mark belongs to that mark alone. Each later `data()`
applies to the mark written directly after it. Two marks draw in the order you
wrote them, so the second sits on top of the first. [Which orders
matter](operators.qmd#which-orders-matter) has all of it in one place.

**Deriving** is what `*` does: it puts a transform on a mark, and the mark is
always on the left. Two transforms can follow one mark: `bar * bin * mean` cuts
the axis into bands, then averages inside each. They have to divide the work,
and each job is filled once, so the order you write them in does not change the
picture. Writing them in the order they happen is the convention.

**Precedence** decides what groups first: `*` and `/`, then `+`, then `|`. In
`data(table) + bar * bin + x(a) | facet(g)`, the transform joins its mark first.
The atoms join the plot next, and the facet splits the finished plot last. So a
single plot needs no parentheses. A page of plots takes one pair of parentheses
around each plot. Julia gives `+` and `|` the same precedence, so there the
parentheses are what keep each plot whole.

**When gog refuses**, the message names the rule, and says what to write
instead. **Illegal** means the grammar forbids the sentence you wrote: rewrite
it. **Unsupported** means the grammar allows it and this engine does not draw
it: use another atom that renders. [Illegal is not the same as
unsupported](design-laws.qmd#illegal-is-not-the-same-as-unsupported) has the
rule, and a live refusal of each kind.

**When gog assumes** instead of refusing, the plot still draws. The message is
an assumption: it says what gog decided for you. Read it, and check that the
decision was what you meant.
